catalog_quote: [p.152, sec. 11 TONE TYPOLOGY] Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. This fact further distances Lakes Plain languages from the Trans New Guinea Phylum. All the modem languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. [p.160, Appendix 3] Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation only: all Lakes Plain languages (Awera included by membership) are tonal with at least H and L; stress has not been found contrastive in any Lakes Plain language. No statement of where stress falls, and nothing Awera-specific on prosody; for Awera the author's only data are a 1987 survey wordlist (p.141 'the only data that do exist are word lists').
new_statements.exceptions: none; Sikaritai analysed as pitch accent (Martin 1991) is the only per-language prosodic qualification, not relevant to Awera
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative overview based on survey word lists; remarks concern transcription conventions for isolated citation forms, not an analysis of Awera word prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Single-village language: Clouse 1997 gives the wordlist village as 'Awera'; the SIL archive record of the same Jones Feb-1987 list gives 'Wapoga Village, Waropen Regency' (Awera village lies in Wapoga District; the village is majority Ansus-speaking per Wikipedia/Clouse). Same variety, glottocode awer1241; no dialects reported.

new_statements.quote: Unlike languages of the Trans-New-Guinea Phylum in the area, tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plains languages and therefore was most likely a feature of PLP as well. All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Sikaritai has only these tones and Martin (1991) analyzes the system as pitch-accent. The remainer of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.), and Iau, because of deleting the segments of a syllable but not the tones, has more than one tone pattern on a syllable.
new_statements.citation: Clouse, Duane. 1993. Languages of the Western Lakes Plains. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya 21: 1-32.
new_statements.locator: sec. 10 'Tone Typology', pp. 19-20 (PDF spread 11 right half / spread 12 left half); the article runs pp. 1-32 and the word 'stress' occurs nowhere in it
new_statements.relation_note: Same family-level tone statement as the existing Clouse 1997 p.152 quote (the 1997 text is a near-verbatim revision of this 1993 passage); the catalog record for Awera has an empty rule and this work adds no placement, so nothing to contradict. Live papuaweb.org does not resolve (DNS, two attempts); opened via the the Internet Archive copy of the papuaweb Irian library (index snapshot 2020-07-11, PDF 20200711062749); whole-volume image-only scan, scanned at native 300 dpi and the deciding passage checked against the page image.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement only: every Lakes Plains language, Awera included, has at least a high/low tonal contrast; nothing is said about stress, and Awera is not named in the tone section (it is mentioned only for segmental facts: initial consonant clusters 'Aw priya' p.10-11, nasals non-contrastive with voiced stops in Awera and Saponi p.11 sec. 3.1, syllable structure p.11 sec. 3.3, reflexes Table 5 p.12). The paper says its Far-West data are wordlists only (p.10-11: 'the only data that do exist are wordlists').
new_statements.exceptions: Sikaritai (not Awera) is said to be analysable as pitch accent (Martin 1991); the sentence about stress not being contrastive that appears in Clouse 1997 Appendix 3 is NOT in this 1993 article
new_statements.identity_note: Clouse 1993 treats Awera as one of three Far-West Lakes Plains languages (with Saponi and Rasawa), data from survey wordlists only; the 'Awera Group' in the endnote (p.27) reproduces Silzer & Clouse 1991's earlier Geelvink Bay Phylum classification. No dialect is distinguished.
